parentTitle: The Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer Care
title: Multimorbidity and complex care coordination
blurb: Use the NICE NG56 approach to reduce treatment burden around the person's goals, and coordinate safe transitions between hospital and home.
question: Mr Desai, 79, has COPD, heart failure, type 2 diabetes and depression, takes 13 regular medicines and attends four different clinics. At his review he says his priority is to keep gardening and stay out of hospital. His HbA1c is slightly above target and a fourth diabetes medicine is suggested. What is the best nursing approach?

teach.body: NICE NG56 defines multimorbidity as the presence of 2 or more long-term health conditions. These include defined physical and mental health conditions (such as diabetes or schizophrenia), ongoing conditions such as learning disability, symptom complexes such as frailty or chronic pain, sensory impairment such as sight or hearing loss, and alcohol and substance misuse. Plain English: the person is more than a list of diseases. Their conditions and treatments interact, and following every single-condition guideline at once can overwhelm them.

teach.h: Why single-condition guidance may not fit
teach.body: NICE warns that the evidence behind single-condition guidance often comes from people without multimorbidity who take fewer medicines. Managing risk factors for future disease can itself be a major treatment burden. So think carefully about the risks and benefits of each recommended treatment for this person, and discuss it with them alongside their preferences.

teach.text: Multimorbidity is not just 'several physical diseases'. Hearing loss plus chronic back pain, or a learning disability plus alcohol misuse, meets the NG56 definition. And agreeing a plan around the person's goals is not 'withholding treatment': it is weighing benefit and burden for this person.

teach.h: Transitions between hospital and home (NICE NG27)

What good looks like

Older people with complex needs: comprehensive assessment from admission
Discharge planning starts on admission; one discharge coordinator
Diagnoses, treatment and a complete medicines list given
Discharge summary to GP within 24 h; copy to person on the day
Long-term care home decisions made while in crisis
teach.caption: NG27 (2015) recs 1.1.5, 1.3.3, 1.3.9–1.3.10, 1.5.1, 1.5.6, 1.5.11.

teach.body: Mr Desai, 79, has COPD, heart failure, type 2 diabetes and depression, takes 13 medicines and attends four clinics. He wants to keep gardening and stay out of hospital. His HbA1c is slightly above target and another diabetes medicine is suggested. The nurse explores his disease and treatment burden, his mood and his goals, then makes sure the benefits and harms of adding a medicine are discussed in light of those goals. The agreed plan names his practice nurse as coordinator, combines appointments where possible and is shared with him and his clinics.

Offer the approach for treatment difficulty, many services, mind and body conditions, frailty or falls, frequent unplanned care or many medicines.
Steps: purpose, burden, goals, review treatments, agree a plan with a named coordinator.

Transitions: information travels with the person, one discharge coordinator, summary to GP within 24 h, no care home decisions in crisis.

summary: You can now recognise multimorbidity, decide who benefits from the NICE NG56 approach and help build an individualised plan around the person's goals. You can also coordinate safe transitions between hospital and home in line with NICE NG27.

A.q: A community nurse is identifying people on her caseload who meet the NICE NG56 definition of multimorbidity. Which person meets it?
options: Mr Hart, 70, with type 2 diabetes and no other conditions
Ms Ford, 45, with a learning disability and sight loss
Mrs Wye, 66, who fractured her wrist last month
Mr Lund, 72, who has had two chest infections this year
A.why: NG56 rec 1.1.1: multimorbidity is 2 or more long-term conditions, which can include ongoing conditions such as learning disability and sensory impairment such as sight loss.

whyNot.0: One long-term condition does not meet the definition of 2 or more.
whyNot.2: A recent fracture is an acute injury, not a long-term condition.
whyNot.3: Repeated acute infections are not long-term conditions in themselves.

A.q: Which finding is one of the NICE NG56 reasons to consider an approach to care that takes account of multimorbidity?
options: Being aged over 75 with two conditions
Having one long-term condition managed by a specialist
Frequently seeking unplanned or emergency care
Having had a recent planned operation
A.why: NG56 rec 1.2.1 lists frequently seeking unplanned or emergency care among the reasons, along with treatment difficulty, multiple services, physical plus mental health conditions, frailty or falls and multiple medicines.

whyNot.0: Age is not one of the NG56 criteria.
whyNot.1: A single condition under a specialist does not meet the criteria.
whyNot.3: A planned operation is not an NG56 criterion.

A.q: During a multimorbidity review, the nurse wants to establish Mr Ray's treatment burden. Which question does this best?
options: How long have you had each of your conditions?
Which of your conditions was diagnosed first?
How do your appointments and medicines affect your day?
What was your most recent blood pressure reading at the clinic?
A.why: NG56 rec 1.6.4: establish treatment burden by talking about how treatments affect day-to-day life, including appointments, medicines, harms and non-drug treatments.

whyNot.0: Duration of conditions does not show how treatment affects his life.
whyNot.1: Order of diagnosis does not measure treatment burden.
whyNot.3: A single reading is clinical data, not his experience of treatment burden.

B.q: In the NICE NG56 approach, which step comes straight after discussing its purpose with the person?
options: Establishing disease and treatment burden
Reviewing medicines and other treatments
Agreeing the individualised management plan
Arranging follow-up and access to urgent care
B.why: NG56 rec 1.5.2 sets the order: discuss the purpose, establish disease and treatment burden, establish goals and priorities, review treatments, then agree the plan.

whyNot.1: Reviewing treatments comes after burden and goals are established.
whyNot.2: The plan is agreed last, once burden, goals and treatments are known.
whyNot.3: Follow-up and urgent care access are part of the final plan.

B.q: Mr Desai, 79, has complex needs and is being discharged after 3 weeks. His family say they have spoken to six different people and do not know who is organising things. What does NICE NG27 recommend?
options: Each team arranges its own part of the discharge
The GP takes over arranging discharge from home
A single practitioner coordinates his discharge
The consultant makes every discharge decision
B.why: NG27 recs 1.5.1–1.5.2: make a single health or social care practitioner responsible for coordinating discharge, as the central point of contact for professionals, the person and family.

whyNot.0: Separate arrangements by each team are what NG27 aims to avoid.
whyNot.1: Discharge coordination sits with a named practitioner, usually hospital or community MDT, not the GP alone.
whyNot.3: The coordinator is involved in all discharge decisions; it is not one consultant deciding everything.

B.q: Mrs Kaur, 86, was admitted 2 days ago and has delirium. Because of bed pressures, a colleague suggests asking her today whether she will move into a care home. What does NICE NG27 advise?
options: Ask her daughter to decide today on her behalf
Make a best-interests decision now to free the bed
Avoid long-term care decisions while she is in crisis
Arrange a temporary care home move without discussion
B.why: NG27 rec 1.5.11: ensure people do not have to make decisions about long-term residential or nursing care while they are in crisis; rec 1.5.12: bed pressures must not drive unplanned discharges.

whyNot.0: A relative cannot simply decide for her; and the decision should not be made during the crisis.
whyNot.1: Bed pressure is not a reason for a long-term decision; NICE warns against this.
whyNot.3: Moving her without discussion ignores her involvement and the advice on crisis decisions.

C.q: Mr Desai, 79, has COPD, heart failure, type 2 diabetes and depression and takes 13 regular medicines. He says his priority is to keep gardening and stay out of hospital. His HbA1c is slightly above target and a fourth diabetes medicine is suggested. What is the best nursing approach?
options: Support adding it, as the single-condition HbA1c target applies to him
Decline it for him, as he already takes too many medicines
Defer every change until his next annual review
Make sure its benefits and harms are discussed with his goals
C.why: NG56 recs 1.1.4 and 1.6.15: think about the risks and benefits of single-condition recommendations for people with multimorbidity and discuss them with the person, taking into account their goals and priorities.

whyNot.0: Single-condition targets may not fit; NICE asks for an individual weighing of benefit and harm.
whyNot.1: The decision is shared with him; the nurse does not decide for him.
whyNot.2: Delaying the discussion leaves the question unresolved; NICE asks for it to be discussed now.

C.q: A GP practice wants to identify, from its records, adults with multimorbidity who are at risk of unplanned hospital admission. What does NICE NG56 suggest?
options: A falls risk prediction tool at reception
A validated tool such as eFI in GP electronic records
NEWS2 recorded at every routine appointment
STOPP/START applied to every registered adult at the practice
C.why: NG56 rec 1.3.2: consider a validated tool such as eFI, PEONY or QAdmissions, if available in primary care records, to identify adults with multimorbidity at risk of adverse events such as unplanned admission.

whyNot.0: NICE advises against falls risk prediction tools (NG249), and they do not identify multimorbidity risk.
whyNot.2: NEWS2 detects acute deterioration, not risk of future admission across a practice list.
whyNot.3: STOPP/START reviews medicines in older people; it is not a population risk tool.

C.q: Mrs Lee, 81, is going home after an admission during which several of her 12 medicines were changed. According to NICE NG27, what should she be given when she leaves?
options: A list of the medicines that were changed
A copy of her ward drug chart to show the GP
Her GP's phone number to ask about any medicine queries at home
Her diagnoses, treatment and a complete medicines list
C.why: NG27 rec 1.1.5: give people information about their diagnoses and treatment and a complete list of their medicines when they transfer between hospital and home (and to family or carers if appropriate).

whyNot.0: A list of changes is incomplete; NICE asks for a complete list of her medicines.
whyNot.1: A drug chart is not the complete, explained list NICE describes.
whyNot.2: Contact details help, but they do not replace the information and medicines list.

reteach.title: Fit the care to the person, not the person to the guidelines
reteach.question: Why might following every guideline for every condition harm someone with five long-term conditions?

blocks.body: Each guideline adds tablets, tests and appointments. Together they can mean 15 medicines, nine clinic visits a month and side effects that cause falls or kidney injury. NG56 asks the team to find out what the person's conditions and treatments do to their daily life, what they want most, and then to agree one plan with one coordinator.

blocks.text: Don't ask someone to decide about a care home while they are acutely unwell or in crisis (NICE NG27 rec 1.5.11).

explain.body: 2 or more long-term conditions: physical and mental health conditions, ongoing conditions such as learning disability, symptom complexes such as frailty or chronic pain, sensory impairment, and alcohol and substance misuse.

test.q: Which of these does NICE NG56 list as a symptom complex that counts towards multimorbidity?
options: Chronic pain
A broken ankle
A urine infection
Seasonal flu
test.why: NG56 rec 1.1.1 names frailty and chronic pain as symptom complexes that count as long-term conditions.

whyNot.1: A fracture is an acute injury.
whyNot.2: A urine infection is an acute illness.
whyNot.3: Seasonal flu is an acute infection.

explain.body: Consider the approach if the person asks, finds treatments or daily activities hard to manage, receives care from several services, has physical and mental health conditions, has frailty or falls, frequently uses unplanned care, or takes many medicines (use at 15+, consider at 10–14).

test.q: Mr Ng, 68, has schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes and is managing well. Why might NICE NG56 suggest considering a multimorbidity approach for him?
options: He is over the age of 65
He has both physical and mental health conditions
He has had type 2 diabetes for longer than 5 years now
He takes fewer than 5 regular medicines
test.why: NG56 rec 1.2.1 lists having both long-term physical and mental health conditions as a reason to consider the approach.

whyNot.0: Age is not an NG56 criterion.
whyNot.2: Duration of diabetes is not an NG56 criterion.
whyNot.3: Few medicines is not a reason; many medicines is.

explain.body: After discussing burden and the person's goals, agree an individualised plan: treatment changes, prioritised appointments, who coordinates care and how that is communicated, follow-up and urgent access. Share it in an accessible format with the person and, with permission, others involved.

test.q: Which item does NICE NG56 include in the individualised management plan?
options: A target to reduce his medicines to under 10
Who is responsible for coordinating his care
A fixed annual review date for each specialty
A rule that he sees one clinician for everything
test.why: NG56 rec 1.6.17: the plan includes assigning responsibility for coordination of care and making sure this is communicated to other professionals and services.

whyNot.0: NICE does not set a numerical medicine target in the plan.
whyNot.2: The plan prioritises appointments around the person; it does not fix one per specialty.
whyNot.3: A coordinator links services; the person still sees the professionals they need.

explain.body: NG27: relevant information, including advance care plans, goes with the person into hospital; discharge planning starts on admission with a single discharge coordinator; the person gets their diagnoses, treatment and a complete medicines list; the GP receives the discharge summary within 24 hours, with a copy to the person on the day.

test.q: Under NICE NG27, by when should the person's GP receive their hospital discharge summary?
options: Within 24 hours of discharge
Within 48 hours of discharge
Within 7 days of discharge
Within 14 days of discharge
test.why: NG27 rec 1.5.6: the discharge summary should be available to the GP within 24 hours of discharge, with a copy given to the person on the day they leave.

whyNot.1: 48 hours is longer than NICE advises.
whyNot.2: 7 days is far longer than the NG27 standard.
whyNot.3: 14 days would leave the GP uninformed during the riskiest period.
